notes.h: Options when buying fruit and vegetables
notes.b: Shoppers can buy fruit and vegetables in several forms, and each has a place in the diet. The best choice depends on cost, time, storage space and how soon the produce will be used.
points: Fresh: choose firm produce with no bruising, cuts, mould, wilting or discolouration, because damage shortens keeping time. In-season produce is usually cheaper and has the best flavour; buy usable quantities and shop often for the most perishable items.

Frozen: picked and frozen soon after harvest, so frozen fruit and vegetables retain most of their nutrients. They are convenient, create little waste, are available all year and can be cooked from frozen. Check the pack is solid, undamaged and not frosted, and that it has been kept frozen.

Canned: cooked and sealed in tins or jars, so the product has a long shelf life and is ready to use. Check the liquid: brine adds salt (canned vegetables often contain added salt) and syrup adds sugar, while juice-packed or water-packed options exist. Check cans for dents, bulges and leaks.

Dried: most of the water is removed, so the produce is light and keeps for long periods. Dried fruit such as raisins and apricots is concentrated in sugar and energy, and dried pulses need soaking or cooking.
Other choices also exist: organic, Fairtrade, loose or pre-packed, in-season or imported (out-of-season) produce, and exotic fruit.
Pre-prepared (convenience) produce is washed, peeled, cut or ready to cook, such as salad bags, stir-fry mixes and fruit salad pots. It saves time and skill and leaves little waste.
The disadvantages of pre-prepared produce are that it costs more, has a shorter shelf life once prepared than whole produce, and some vitamin C is lost through cutting.

When buying pre-prepared produce, check the use-by or best-before date, cost and value for money, that the packaging is undamaged and unopened, that there is no discolouration or sliminess, that the quantity suits the household, the storage and cooking instructions, and the nutritional information on the label.
notes.tip: For a question on the options available, cover fresh, frozen, canned, dried and pre-prepared, then add organic, Fairtrade, in and out of season, loose or packaged, and exotic. On pre-prepared produce, give each factor (such as date, cost, intact package) one extra point to earn the marks.

notes.b: Two shoppers can make different choices from the same shelf, because their circumstances differ. Cost, skills, time and storage space decide how much is bought fresh, frozen or pre-prepared.
points: Cost: buying in season is cheaper, loose produce is cheaper than packaged, and buying direct from growers or markets can save money.
Buying in bulk only makes sense if there is freezer or preserving capacity, because fresh produce left over will spoil.
Skills and time: the household's cooking skills and the time available decide how much is bought fresh and how much pre-prepared.
Storage space (fridge, freezer, cool dry store) limits the quantity that can be bought and kept in good condition.
notes.tip: Questions on what influences a shopper buying fresh produce look for cost, skills, time and storage space, each with a short reason.

notes.b: Shoppers judge quality by looking, feeling and smelling, and the EU sets grading classes so that buyers know what standard they are getting. Fresh fruit and vegetables sold in the EU must meet marketing standards.
points: Quality signs when selecting fresh produce: firmness, fresh colour, crispness, no bruising or blemish, no mould or sprouting, uniform size (for even cooking), fresh-looking stalks and leaves, a pleasant smell, and heavy for its size.
Extra class: the best (superior) quality, uniform in shape, size and colour, and free from defects.
Class I: good quality, with minor defects allowed provided they do not affect general appearance, keeping quality or presentation; it is free from bruising and has only slight defects.
Class II: reasonably good, acceptable quality, with more defects of shape or colour allowed, but still fit for consumption. It is sound and good for cooking and processing.
The grading standards are the EU marketing standards for fresh produce, set in Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2429.
Fresh produce must show its country of origin under these marketing standards and, where the standard requires it, the class and variety.
Irish produce may carry the Bord Bia quality assurance mark, which shows it has met an assured standard. This mark is a quality assurance scheme and is not the same thing as an EU class.
notes.tip: There are three current classes: Extra, I and II. When asked to identify and explain two classes, name each and state its defect allowance, as in the points above.

notes.h: Effects of storage: why produce changes
notes.b: Fruit and vegetables are still alive after harvest, so they keep changing while they wait to be sold and eaten. This is why storage guidelines exist.
points: Produce keeps respiring (using up its own food reserves), losing moisture and ripening after harvest, so quality and vitamin C fall with time.
For this reason, buy little and often, use produce soon, and rotate older stock to the front so it is used first.

Fresh vegetables should be refrigerated at about 5 degrees Celsius or below and used as soon as possible, because vitamin C declines during storage. This applies to refrigerated salad and vegetables, not to produce such as potatoes and onions that is kept in a cool store.
notes.tip: Exams ask you to describe or outline three storage guidelines. Pick three different items, for example potatoes dark and dry, wrapping removed and veg in the drawer, and apples kept apart, and give the reason for each.

notes.b: Different produce needs different conditions. The aim is to slow moisture loss, ripening and rot without damaging the produce.
points: Salad and most fresh vegetables: remove any plastic wrapping and damaged items, then store in the refrigerator in the salad or vegetable drawer with air circulating, and use quickly. A sealed bag traps condensation, which speeds rot.

Potatoes: store in a cool, dark, dry, ventilated place such as a vegetable rack or paper sack. Light turns them green and produces bitter solanine, which is harmful, so discard green or sprouting parts or tubers.
Onions and root vegetables: store in a cool, dry, dark, ventilated place, because damp conditions encourage rot. Keep the tops of roots trimmed.
Apples and bananas give off ethylene, a gas that speeds the ripening of nearby produce, so keep them away from other fruit and vegetables.

Bananas and other tropical fruit, and hard fruit, ripen at room temperature, away from ethylene producers. Soft fruit and berries are then refrigerated, and berries are washed only just before eating.
Keep fresh produce away from raw meat and fish to prevent cross-contamination, wash produce before use, and clean the fridge regularly.
notes.tip: Two common slips: take off plastic wrapping rather than storing salad in a sealed bag, and give the reason for keeping potatoes in the dark (solanine).

notes.h: Storage of frozen, canned and dried produce
notes.b: Processed produce keeps longer, but only if the storage conditions are right. The rules protect both quality and safety.
points: Frozen: store at minus 18 degrees Celsius or below, wrapped in moisture-proof packaging, and use within the date. Do not refreeze after thawing.
Canned: keep in a cool, dry place. Once a can is opened, transfer the contents to a covered container in the fridge and use within a day or two.
Dented, swollen (bulging) or leaking cans are discarded, because they may be unsafe.
Dried fruit is kept in a sealed container in a cool, dry place.

notes.b: Enzymes (proteins in the produce that speed up chemical reactions) stay active after harvest. They cause two kinds of spoilage: ripening that goes too far, and browning of cut surfaces.
points: Enzymes remain active after harvesting and continue the ripening process until the produce becomes over-ripe, soft and eventually decays.
When cells are cut, bruised or peeled, the enzyme oxidase is released and reacts with oxygen in the air, causing enzymic browning, as seen in apple, potato and banana.
Enzymic browning also destroys some vitamin C and carotene.
Cold slows the enzymes, so refrigeration slows ripening and browning.

Blanching before freezing (brief boiling water, then cold) denatures the enzymes, which means their shape is destroyed so they stop working. Unblanched vegetables continue to deteriorate even in a freezer.
Acid such as lemon juice lowers the pH and slows browning.
Excluding air, for example with water, sugar syrup or wrapping, stops oxygen reaching the cut surface.
notes.tip: For a cut apple turning brown, name the enzyme (oxidase) and oxygen. When asked to explain two ways to control enzymic spoilage, choose from blanching, cold or acid and say how each works.

notes.b: Fresh produce is mostly water, so losing it changes how it looks and feels. Loss is fastest in warm, dry, uncovered storage.
points: Moisture is lost through respiration and evaporation, especially in warm, dry, uncovered storage.
Loss of water causes cells to lose turgor (the firmness that water pressure gives cells), so leafy vegetables wilt, roots shrivel and skins wrinkle.
Produce loses mass and becomes limp, with poorer texture and appearance.
Cool, humid storage such as a salad drawer, and suitable packaging, slow moisture loss.
Covering cut produce and not leaving produce in warm rooms also reduces loss.
notes.tip: Moisture loss answers need a mechanism, an effect and a control: water lost, cells lose turgor so produce wilts, and humid storage slows it.

notes.b: Micro-organisms are tiny living things such as bacteria, yeasts and moulds. They use the produce as food, and their growth makes it unfit to eat.
points: Bacteria, yeasts and moulds come from soil, water, dirty hands and equipment, pests, damaged produce and cross-contamination.
Bruises and cuts give micro-organisms access to nutrients and moisture inside the produce.
Warmth, moisture, food (the produce itself), time and a suitable pH allow micro-organisms to multiply rapidly.
Bacteria cause soft, slimy rot and unpleasant odours; moulds form coloured fuzzy growth, and some produce harmful mycotoxins (poisons).
Yeasts ferment the sugars in fruit, giving a sour or alcoholic smell and bubbles.

Prevention combines good hygiene (clean hands, equipment and surfaces), removing damaged items, separating produce from raw meat, careful washing, refrigeration, correct storage temperatures and prompt use. Washing alone is not enough, because soil-borne contamination can persist.
Other causes of spoilage are physical damage, such as bruising or crushing in transport, and pests.
notes.tip: In a discussion of causes of spoilage, the three headings are enzymes, moisture loss and micro-organisms. For micro-organisms give the sources, the conditions they need, the effect (rot or mould) and the prevention.

notes.b: Businesses that handle produce are bound by hygiene law, and public bodies oversee food safety. Grading is set at EU level.
points: Food businesses must follow the hygiene rules in Regulation (EC) No 852/2004, given effect in Ireland by the European Communities (Hygiene of Foodstuffs) Regulations 2006.

The Food Safety Authority of Ireland (FSAI), established under the Food Safety Authority of Ireland Act 1998, enforces food law through service contracts and gives food safety guidance on handling and storing produce.

keyTerms.definition: The brown discolouration of cut or bruised produce caused by oxidase reacting with oxygen.
Brief immersion of vegetables in boiling water, followed by rapid cooling, before freezing.
The pressure of water inside plant cells that keeps leaves and stems firm; loss of turgor causes wilting.
A toxic substance produced by some moulds growing on food.
The highest EU marketing grade for fresh fruit and vegetables, uniform and free from defects.
A gas given off by ripening fruit such as apples, which speeds the ripening of nearby produce.
The transfer of micro-organisms from raw food, surfaces or hands to food that will not be cooked.
The continued breakdown of stored sugars in harvested produce, which releases water and heat.

factCards.term: Three causes of spoilage in vegetables
factCards.definition: Enzymes, moisture loss and microbial contamination.

factCards.term: Storage temperature for frozen fruit and vegetables
Three EU marketing grades for fresh produce
factCards.definition: Extra, Class I and Class II.

factCards.term: Two effects of long storage on fresh vegetables
factCards.definition: Vitamin C is lost, and texture and appearance deteriorate.

factCards.term: Why blanching is done before freezing
factCards.definition: It denatures enzymes that would otherwise cause deterioration during freezer storage.

factCards.term: Produce that should be kept apart from apples
factCards.definition: Vegetables, because apples release ethylene, which speeds up their ripening.

factCards.term: Main nutritional drawback of dried fruit
factCards.definition: It is concentrated in sugar and energy because most of its water has been removed.

factCards.term: Hazard that causes mould growth on stored vegetables
factCards.definition: Mycotoxins are produced by some moulds, and bruised or damaged produce allows moulds to grow.

questions.prompt: Outline two reasons why fresh vegetables lose quality during storage.
questions.model: Any two: vitamin C declines with time in storage; moisture is lost by respiration and evaporation, so vegetables wilt and lose texture; enzymes continue ripening and softening until the produce decays; micro-organisms multiply, especially where produce is damaged or stored warm.

questions.prompt: Describe how enzymes, moisture loss and micro-organisms each reduce the quality of stored fresh vegetables, and explain the storage and handling measures that prevent each cause.
questions.model: Enzymes: continue ripening after harvest, softening the produce until it decays; oxidase released from cut or bruised cells causes enzymic browning and destroys some vitamin C; prevention is prompt use, refrigeration and blanching before freezing. Moisture loss: respiration and evaporation lower cell turgor, so leafy vegetables wilt, roots shrivel and produce loses mass and texture; prevention is humid refrigerated storage, suitable packaging that does not trap condensation and avoiding warm, dry, uncovered storage. Micro-organisms: bacteria, yeasts and moulds enter from soil, hands, equipment, pests and damaged produce; bruises give access to nutrients and moisture; warmth and time allow rapid growth; bacteria cause soft slimy rot and moulds cause coloured fuzzy growth and mycotoxins; prevention is hygiene, removing damaged items, separating produce from raw meat, refrigeration at about 5 degrees Celsius or below and prompt use.
